question_text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician for a 3-week history of intermittent episodes of dizziness. The episodes last for hours at a time and are characterized by the sensation that the room is spinning. The patient also reports that she has started using her cell phone with her left ear because she hears better on that side. She has experienced intermittent ringing and fullness in her right ear. She has no history of serious medical conditions. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F) pulse is 76/min respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. There is horizontal nystagmus to the right. Motor strength is 5/5 in all extremities, and sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal bilaterally. Weber test shows lateralization to the left ear. The Rinne test is positive bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

                    ### Question
                    A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician for a 3-week history of intermittent episodes of dizziness. The episodes last for hours at a time and are characterized by the sensation that the room is spinning. The patient also reports that she has started using her cell phone with her left ear because she hears better on that side. She has experienced intermittent ringing and fullness in her right ear. She has no history of serious medical conditions. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. She takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F) pulse is 76/min respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/76 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. There is horizontal nystagmus to the right. Motor strength is 5/5 in all extremities, and sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal bilaterally. Weber test shows lateralization to the left ear. The Rinne test is positive bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Demyelinating plaques
opb. Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery
opc. Reduced resorption of endolymph
opd. Cerebellopontine angle tumor
ope. Obstruction of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms of intermittent dizziness, sensation of the room spinning, hearing better on the left side, ringing and fullness in the right ear, and horizontal nystagmus to the right, along with the Weber test lateralizing to the left and positive Rinne test bilaterally, are most consistent with Meniere's disease. This condition is characterized by episodes of vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, typically due to reduced resorption of endolymph in the inner ear. The evidence path mentioning horizontal nystagmus as a symptom aligns with this diagnosis, although the broader context of menopause and hand location is not directly relevant. Other options, such as cerebellopontine angle tumor or vascular occlusions, are less likely given the specific combination of auditory and vestibular symptoms without additional neurological deficits. Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is reduced resorption of endolymph, consistent with Meniere's disease.
